chapters.summary: Chair Justin E. Sanchez welcomes attendees and jokes about a cyber attack on the Committee on Sanitation. He then turns the floor over to Council Member Kayla Santosuosso for questions.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez opens hearing with humor about cyber attack

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us through the Committee on Sanitation's cyber attack.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: They were so much highly sensitive information and snow materials being discussed that, you know, Los Angeles really...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Came for us.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: They needed all of our snow knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Having said that, I will now turn it over to Council Member Sanchez-Woso for some questions.

chapters.summary: Council Member Kayla Santosuosso acknowledges a constituent killed by a sanitation truck, then asks about corner property responsibility for clearing pedestrian ramps. She raises concerns about plowed snow piling at crosswalks and asks about strategies to ensure entire crosswalks are cleared. DSNY officials describe prioritizing corners near bus stops and subway stops, and using emergency snow shovelers.
chapters.title: Santosuosso questions DSNY on pedestrian ramp and crosswalk snow clearing

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And before I start with questions, I just want to acknowledge the constituent who was killed in my district last week by a sanitation truck.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I know the incident is still under investigation.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: We'll have lots of time to discuss what could have been done, but I appreciate so much the early outreach by you, Commissioner, and your commitment to finding out whatever we can do to prevent that from happening again.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I want to ask...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Primarily when it comes to snow clearing.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: We've established, I think, as a result of the last hearing, that the corner property is responsible for clearing a pedestrian ramp.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Corner property is responsible for clearing a path to and including a pedestrian ramp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That is largely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I think at the last hearing we discussed, and I don't believe you had been appointed yet, and so my sort of pet peeve last year, because of everyone pushing a stroller and having accessibility issues, is that people were clearing the corner.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: A path to the corner and clearing the ped ramp, but then sanitation was plowing snow such that it piled up right at the end of the crosswalk.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So there would be a mound of snow in between the crosswalk where people were crossing and then the properly cleared, hopefully, pedestrian ramp.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Hopefully we don't get that level of snow again such that it has mounds sort of staying on the street But at the time the acting commissioner was looking into ways that we could

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Sort of make sure that the entire crosswalk was cleared particularly when the corner property is doing their their piece in clearing the ped ramp Wondering if there's a strategy this year around around that

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so to start, I think that's where having the emergency snow shoveler program be much more robust and also having more snow blowers and other equipment to be able to respond to those areas more quickly will be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've also done a lot of work in routing to those corners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're trying to avoid this distinction between it's a ped ramp versus it's a crosswalk versus we're just treating everything on the corner that connects the sidewalk to the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: street as a corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And if we get there and it's not shoveled, we will shovel it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we get there and it's shoveled, great, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the thing that we're doing differently from a routing perspective this year is we are trying to prioritize which corners we are doing first with our snow shovelers and our sanitation workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a couple different criteria that we're using to prioritize those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The first is any corner that is within 200 feet of a bus stop or a subway stop is getting prioritized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Any corner that is on DOT has a sort of five-tier ranking of crosswalks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Any corner that's in the top three tiers of those rankings, which is the areas that have the highest number of pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those are prioritized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're also looking at corners that have the accessible pedestrian indicators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So those are the audible indicators for the crosswalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those are all prioritized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In total, it comes out to around 20,000 corners, which we understand is still a very small share of all of the corners in New York City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think there's never a world where we are going to get to everything as a number one priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we have to do some prioritization based on where the most people are moving in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, in the days immediately after a storm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And one of the things that we are also doing is working with the mayor's office for people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and the Department for the Aging to make sure that we are also prioritizing areas where we know there are high populations of people with mobility challenges or who rely on mobility devices to get around so that we are also accounting for that.

chapters.summary: Council Member Santosuosso notes that schools were a major concern for constituents. She asks about ensuring corners near schools are clear during drop-off and dismissal. DSNY officials say they work closely with NYC Public Schools custodial staff and coordinate on routes to schools.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about clearing snow around schools

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: If I may, I mean, it sounds like you've sort of worked out that priority structure, but schools were also what I heard the most of.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And granted, I know it's mostly DOE's responsibility to clear outside of school sites, but making sure those corners are clear given the heavy pedestrian traffic, especially during dismissal and drop-off as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think the New York City Public Schools custodial staff do tremendous work to get schools back open, often in the hours or less than a day after the snowfall ends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think the thing that we try to work very close with them on is making sure that the routes to get to that school, either from the nearest public transit stop or from where parents or buses are dropping off, are also clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's not just the sidewalk immediately proximate to the school, but it's the larger area around the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's something that we work very closely with Kevin Moran, who's their chief operating officer, and his team on.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thanks, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez recognizes Council Members Vernikov and Ressler. Council Member Carl Wilson then asks about standards for clearing pedestrian intersections and ramps with the new robust shoveler team. He also asks about 311 guidance on reporting bus shelter clearing. DSNY officials say they are still building the workforce and cannot commit to specific response times.
chapters.title: Wilson questions DSNY on pedestrian access standards and 311 complaints

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize that we've been joined by Councilmember Vernikov on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I don't think I said Councilmember Ressler earlier, but I want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And now we will.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Turn it over to Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Hello, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Just to follow up about the pedestrian access, is with this new robust team of shovelers,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: is there a certain standard that you expect to be able to have pedestrian side intersections and ped ramps cleared that perhaps you weren't able to have in the last time?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And also, if, sorry, I lost my train of thought.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: When you, 311 says that I think you have to wait like 72 hours before reporting or accepting complaints about bus shelters being cleared.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Do you expect that to remain the same, given the new robust workforce that you have doing some of the shoveling?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I'll start by saying the robust workforce that we expect to have is one that we are still working to build.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we need the help of not only every city council member, but every other elected official and community leader to help us get to

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the level of pre-registration for snow shovelers that we need in order to be able to mount a really robust response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we have more time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's still 60 degrees out right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's only November 2nd, but snow will be here before we know it, and we need to continue working in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As far as a specific expectation around when certain assets will be cleared, I think it's far too dependent on the characteristics of an individual snowstorm, the temperatures leading into it, the amount of snow that's already on the ground, and lots of other factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I don't think we can commit to a specific response time for every single corner in the city or every single bus stop in the city, except that we will respond faster than we have in the past, and we are tracking it much better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we know, as the Department of Sanitation,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: which assets have been cleared by our staff or by our snow shovelers and which have not, and we'll be able to sort of move through the whole set of assets more strategically after the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What was the other question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I think you...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Answered it.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: It was just about like the time response times and what you expect the season.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wilson asks about conflicting policies on bike lane clearing, noting the snow plan says bike lanes are treated simultaneously with roadways while 311 guidance says they are cleared after streets. DSNY officials say the 311 language is out of date and they deploy 47 plow units for bike lanes, using salting for traction.
chapters.title: Wilson questions DSNY on bike lane snow clearing policy

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The so ask about bike lanes for a second.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So the 20 the DSMY 2526 snow plan committed to treating bike lanes simultaneously with roadways.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: But I think there's some 311 guidance describes clearing bike lanes after streets and says that the clearance is not guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So could you clarify which policy?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: We can expect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so that 311 language is clearly out of date, and we'll make sure that we go in and clean that up, because we have 47 plow units on hand that we deploy actually generally before the snow starts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have tried in the past brining bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We find that salting bike lanes works better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It also gives good traction for people who have to use bike lanes to get around even during the snowfall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we have that equipment out and assigned two routes while it's snowing, after it's done snowing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are situations where if a bike lane is blocked by a car or if it's inaccessible for some reason and gets really heavy accumulations, it can be very difficult and very slow work to shovel that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: using either manual shovels or our skid steers or other small equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so, you know, one of the things that I personally, not in this role, but as a New Yorker, observed last year in the January storm was some protected bike lanes that were not able to be serviced during the storm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Were then, you know, unfortunately full of snow that turned into a block of ice and there was really no digging them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think one of the things that we're trying to do this year is have better situational awareness about where our small plows are not able to get into the bike lanes during a storm and try to respond to that either by removing vehicles or towing people out of there.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And do you feel like you have enough equipment of the appropriate sized equipment to be able to deal with the bike lanes?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I think we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Certainly something that we're looking at as DOT is working on their updated streets master plan and they're planning around additional

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: bike infrastructure, additional pedestrian infrastructure is planning proactively so that we are buying new equipment in advance of them installing new capital assets instead of the other way around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For a long time, we sort of played catch up after DOT would build a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We'd say we need resources to take care of that thing and there's a 12 month gap between

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the thing existing and us having the resources to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're trying to get ahead of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And hopefully in the context of the budget, that's something that we're able to talk more about next year.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wilson asks how DSNY will handle snow removal with permanent year-round street dining structures. DSNY officials say they have experience from the temporary COVID program and work with FDNY and DOT to ensure plows can navigate and turn around structures.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about snow removal around street dining structures

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And then,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I think over the winter months we can begin to anticipate more street bed dining structures emerging.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How are you anticipating dealing with that new challenge in the street when it comes to snow removal?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's a new challenge in that they are authorized for permanent year-round placement, but we did deal with four years of the temporary COVID pandemic program,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and there were far more dining sheds out in the streets than there are today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think we have a good approach as far as making sure that our routes can accommodate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a really good relationship with our sister agencies at FDNY and DOT as far as reviewing placement, making sure there's adequate room to get

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: our vehicles through, and most importantly, adequate room for our vehicles to be able to turn, because a collection truck with a plow on it does have a wider turning radius than just a standard collection truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we need to make sure that we can get our plows into blocks, that we can safely plow through the block, and I think we'll be in a good place this year.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez introduces Council Member Shanel Thomas-Henry. She asks about residents in alleyways who were unaware they needed to move trash to the front during snowstorms. DSNY officials say they will be more proactive in notifying residents via social media, text, and possibly mailers.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions DSNY on alleyway trash collection during snowstorms

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And next we will hear from Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: My first question is as it relates to alleyways.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Last season, we saw an accumulation of trash behind homes in their alleyways because residents weren't aware that they needed to place them in front of their homes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And these are residents who had lived there for decades.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What triggers the moving the trash from behind your house in the alleyway to the front yard, and how will those residents be alerted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that's something that I very much want to do differently this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In the past, I think we've relied too much on people just assuming the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And this year, I think we would like to be more clear and more proactive about telling people alley service is suspended, effective on X date, and will not resume for at least Y number of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So looking at the January storm, for example, from last year, we would say very proactively to people, alley service is suspended effective the day prior to the snowstorm happening, and then tell people it will not resume

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: until we tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Last year, unfortunately, because these alleys are not serviced by us for snow removal purposes, they are private streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Many of them were impassable and it was unsafe for us to put equipment back there for over two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think we just need to be clear with folks that if you have private alley service, you need to move your trash to the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the front of your building, it may be two, three weeks in a row, but at least then the trash isn't piling up.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And what way are you going to notify those residents?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How are you going to notify them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're going to be much more proactive on our social media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're also in the process of planning.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: A mailer maybe?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like some of the residents I'm talking about are older adults.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We can take a look at a mailer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think that may be an effective tool, but I think we want to be able to provide more real-time information to folks also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're looking at text message, calling, emailing options to be able to say specifically to those alley service residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Put it out in the front or, you know, on a date certain, alley service will resume.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I name that because my 90-year-old grandmother is one of those, and she can't check email and is not on social media.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Maybe the Facebook, but...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Interesting.

chapters.summary: Council Member Thomas-Henry asks if DSNY will proactively educate property owners about their snow removal responsibilities after many received fines. DSNY officials say they do communicate responsibilities and issued over 19,000 violations last year, but could have issued more with more resources.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about fines and property owner snow removal responsibilities

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Along those same lines with just notification, a lot of homeowners and businesses also received fines last year because they weren't aware of exactly how much of their perimeter or adjacent to their property they needed to shovel.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are you guys going to do the same kind of proactive just campaign letting?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Reinforcing to property owners and business owners what they're responsible for?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do a lot of communication to folks on what their responsibilities are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think that, you know, their responsibilities have not generally changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You are, if you own

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: property or are a commercial establishment, you are responsible for clearing your sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that means clearing at least a four foot wide path, clearing a path to the bus stop, clearing around fire hydrants, clearing the pedestrian ramp, that all of that is part of the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And you're responsible for doing so within a certain number of hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: After the snow stops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We usually give people a good amount of leeway, but last year we did issue over 19,000 violations over the two storms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I think that at the end of the day, we probably could have issued another 100,000 more if we had the resources to do so.

chapters.summary: Council Member Thomas-Henry asks who is responsible for clearing access to schools adjacent to parks. DSNY officials say schools clear around schools, Parks Department clears around parks, and they hope the agencies coordinate, with DSNY helping if needed.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about interagency responsibilities for schools adjacent to parks

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to clarify, just clarity on interagency responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have quite a few

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: schools that are adjacent to parks.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In those instances, who is responsible for clearing access in and out of the school?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the school is responsible for clearing the sidewalk around the school itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The park is, the parks department is responsible for clearing around the park.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our hope is that those two agencies are coordinating that together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And if either of them needs additional resources or help to make sure that we're ready to open up school in the morning, we're always happy to help where we can if we have additional resources available.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Gotcha.

chapters.summary: Council Member Thomas-Henry asks about NYC Service's work with local nonprofits and CBOs to help seniors and disabled residents clear snow. DSNY officials explain the program connects volunteers to those in need, but property owners remain responsible. She requests a list of participating nonprofits.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about nonprofit snow removal assistance

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And then in the plan, it mentions NYC services, capacity, resources are given to local nonprofits and CBOs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What does that mean in terms of?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so New York City Service works with community-based organizations to develop community networks where if there's an older New Yorker or a person with disabilities who's unable to shovel their own sidewalk,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: those community organizations can try to connect them to volunteers from the community who are ready, willing, and able to do that work for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That said...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Every New Yorker who owns a property or a commercial establishment is responsible for their sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it is critical for all New Yorkers'ability to move around following a snowstorm that they clear their sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And just because you're an older New Yorker,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and may not be physically able to does not alleviate that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is there a listing of the local nonprofits that you guys work with?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we can work with NYC Service to get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez follows up on neighbor-helping-neighbor efforts, asking if DSNY would develop its own program or volunteer registry to assist seniors and disabled residents. DSNY officials say their priority is public assets, and private property owners are expected to arrange for clearance.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez asks about DSNY program for seniors and disabled New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: To follow up on that, in its draft snow plans, the department encourages neighbors to help each other remove snow when needed.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: However, we know this does not always happen in practice.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has the department considered developing its own program to assist seniors and disabled New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Could emergency snow shovelers be deployed to prioritize accessible transportation routes?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Would the department consider creating its own volunteer registry similar to the city's Adopt-A-Rain Garden program?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So our priority following a snowstorm is public assets, and we assign the resources that we have, both sanitation workers and our emergency snow shovelers, to clear those public assets first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we get to a place where all of the public assets citywide have been cleared, then we can assign them to private assets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I think that would be far too slow for those properties to be cleared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so our expectation is private property owners arrange for the clearance of their properties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, that's an obligation that comes with owning property in New York City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And unfortunately, that's, you know, that's our expectation for folks.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez introduces Council Member Ty Hankerson. He asks about DSNY's work with the Parks Department for clearing public assets. DSNY officials say Parks employees sometimes work alongside sanitation and assign plow operators during snowstorms.
chapters.title: Hankerson questions DSNY on coordination with Parks Department

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, I will turn it over to Councilmember Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you for hearing Intro 1042 today.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I just want to say briefly, one thing that I'm big on is transparency, and I believe that the difference between making information publicly available and making it accessible is necessary and needed for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But for my questioning, Commissioner,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I know we have the emergency snow shovelers program, but are there times where you work with the Parks Department for clearing public assets?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The Parks Department is responsible for clearing their assets, and we are responsible for clearing many of ours.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Is it just parks that they clear, or are they responsible for other city property outside of the parks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There have been times that parks employees have also worked alongside sanitation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They regularly assign plow operators to the sanitation department during snowstorms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And once the parks infrastructure was all cleared last year, I think they did expand to some other public assets.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In those instances, who gives them directives?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Who gives the parks employees directives?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's a combination of parks supervision and sanitation supervision.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Who gives the emergency snow shovelers directives?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Generally, sanitation and DOT workers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are they oftentimes, or in those instances, are they assigned to do similar or different things?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The same work?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Many of the parks employees are still assigned doing parks work within their parks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Parks has probably thousands of miles of paths and sidewalks they're responsible for, so there's quite a good deal of work to do.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hankerson asks if Parks workers doing similar work to emergency snow shovelers should be paid comparably. DSNY officials note emergency snow shovelers are paid $30/hour, while Parks employees are full-time with benefits, so it's not apples to apples.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about pay rates for emergency snow shovelers vs. Parks workers

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are they paid at a comparable rate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, I'm not familiar with exactly the pay rate that most parks employees work, but I know for our emergency snow shoveler program, we did increase the pay rate to $30 an hour,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: in part in recognition of the emergency nature of the work and the fact that we are asking people who aren't full-time employees of the city of New York to come in and do work for us.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If parks workers are completing the same type of work as an emergency snow shoveler or a sanitation worker, do you think they should be paid at a comparable rate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I can't speak to the nature of the compensation and benefits offered to Parks Department employees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They are full-time employees that have pensions and health insurance and other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, I don't know that it's necessarily apples to apples.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hankerson asks if sanitation workers and Parks workers could be assigned together on routes. DSNY officials say generally not side by side, as sanitation workers operate mechanical equipment like plows and skid steers, while emergency snow shovelers do manual work.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about assignments of sanitation workers and Parks workers

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: This is, and this is forgive my ignorance, but when a sanitation worker is assigned a certain route,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: let's just say it's off the snow plow, it's actually shoveling, could they be assigned or could a parks worker be assigned with them on that route?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Not generally side by side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our sanitation workers often are operating mechanical equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As I mentioned in testimony, we have 120 new snow plows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have over 100 skid steers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have the 47 bike lane plows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So generally our sanitation workers, because they're professional drivers, will be assigned to operate equipment where the emergency snow shovelers will do more of the manual work.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hankerson asks why residents cannot access historical GPS plowing data directly through the Plow NYC website. DSNY officials say it is technologically feasible but requires development resources and time.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about public access to Plow NYC historical data

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And finally, just going back to the bill.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: During previous snowstorms, Plow NYC did not allow our office to easily review streets plowing history from the previous day.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If DSNY maintains historical GPS records, why can't residents access that information directly through the public-facing website?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think that's something that we are open to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's just a question of the resources necessary to do that and to build it out in the manner that the bill...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sets forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, it's technologically feasible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's just a question of putting the development resources and time into it.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yep.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez introduces Council Member Lincoln Restler. He raises concerns about impassable intersections and asks about new technology approaches like Montreal's sidewalk clearing. DSNY officials say Montreal clears only a small portion of the city and that clearing all sidewalks would require enormous resources.
chapters.title: Restler questions DSNY on intersection clearing and new technology

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Council Member Ressa.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And good to see you, Commissioner and team.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It was great to have you in Brooklyn Heights last week.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we are really excited about commercial waste zones in CB1.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So there's great things happening with the Department of Sanitation across District 33.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up on one of the items that Councilmember Santos-Woso was highlighting.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Which is just my concern around intersections.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And, you know, it's...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For sure, for people with disabilities, I see the world anew as a young dad trying to get a stroller around.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the number of complaints I got this past year was the sanitation department did an amazing job clearing the streets, and the intersections were totally impassable, so cars could get anywhere they needed to go, but people were utterly screwed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just, you know.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I appreciate a committed effort to having a workforce that's out there to clear intersections and crosswalks

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and that we want property owners on the corners to do more, although I think that's unlikely to change much from what we saw this past winter.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I was wondering if you're considering any new technology approaches.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm sure you're always looking at what other cities in the Northeast are doing and how they clear snow.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Montreal.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Clear sidewalks with, you know, motorized devices.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that something that you think we should consider in New York City?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So a lot of people make a comparison to Montreal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Montreal clears sidewalks in a very small portion of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the level of service they provide is similar to what our business improvement districts are providing in commercial corridors all around the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The city of Montreal is not clearing a standard residential sidewalk in, you know, the sort of far reaches of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think that the resources that would be required for the city to provide that service to every single property that's more than 800,000 property citywide would be enormous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think it is appropriate for that to be the responsibility of the private property owner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And certainly we at the Department of Sanitation are stepping up our capacity to be able to clear the areas that are outside of that private property responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The area from the corner into the crosswalk, the area around the bus stop, making sure that people can continue to keep moving around New York.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: city, however they move.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But even still, in a best-case scenario, I don't know what you're, when you were doing the model, the tabletop exercise this weekend, how long, in a best-case scenario, you said you would hope to do 20,000 intersections.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Did I hear that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How long do you think it would take to do 20,000 intersections if you're fully staffed up and things go as well as possible?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it depends on the weather, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we're operating in 40 degrees the day after a snowstorm, which oftentimes it is 40 degrees the day after a snowstorm, I think we could get to those 20,000 corners within a day or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think if we're in another situation where there's prolonged extreme cold,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, it may take us longer to get to those 20,000 intersection or 20,000 corners, but we would certainly,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think, one, have better situational awareness around what we've achieved and what we haven't, and two, be able to more clearly communicate that to the public.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, I think we just...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In last year's winter, in last year's storms, which were really bad, we saw intersections that were impassable for many days and in like the heart of our commercial districts in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so it was challenging for everybody to get around and, you know, waiting days to be able to walk

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: safely around the neighborhood is really tough.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so, you know, I appreciate the focus on bringing on a greater

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: workforce that can do this work quickly, I remain concerned that we're going to be in tough situations as, you know, the nature of climate change is more extreme weather and more intense storms that are challenging for us to wrestle with.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think we need to think about new approaches that can actually meet these new climate dynamics.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so, you know, whether...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My mom is from Montreal.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm a half Canadian.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I spend a lot of time up there.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think you're, you know, they do a really impressive job clearing a ton of snow all the time.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I do think there are more lessons for us to learn.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Montreal is broken into different municipalities within the city, so it is a different structure.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But in the heart of Montreal, in their downtown area, they clear snow off sidewalks and make it passable in real time.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I just hope that we can do more, especially in our dense urban areas of the city.

chapters.summary: Council Member Restler complains that DOT does not clear snow on BQE bridges and overpasses in his district, forcing him to shovel himself. He asks if DSNY could take responsibility. DSNY officials say they help when asked but prioritize bus stops and 20,000 priority corners.
chapters.title: Restler presses DSNY on snow clearing on BQE bridges and overpasses

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Also just want to take this opportunity to ask you a little bit about one of my kind of chronic snow issues, which are the DOT bridges and the kind of underpasses.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I represent the BQE through much of the northern half of Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Critical for my constituents to be able to walk down the sidewalks on the BQE.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's often, nobody takes responsibility for it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Not sanitation, not DOT.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think it's supposed to be DOT's responsibility, but they never do anything.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so could sanitation take responsibility for clearing the snow off of all bridges?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that in the sidewalk areas?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: that are on those bridges?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that something you all would consider?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or what other options do we have if DOT is going to continue to do nothing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I think DOT actually does a fair bit of work to try to clear overpasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Not in my district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That said, there are a lot of overpasses all across the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so I can't speak to exactly how they prioritize that work, but certainly when they've come to us saying we need help on these locations,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we have the ability to provide that help, we do so.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There has not been a storm in the five years that I've been in the city council where I haven't had to go out myself and shovel on those BQE bridges because DOT is nowhere to be found.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And that's like I'm happy to help in whatever way I can, but that's a pretty absurd process that I'm the one going out there with a shovel.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I don't know how they're prioritizing it, but they're not doing anything in District 33.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I've asked three commissioners over five years and begged for help, and it never seems to come.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So is there a different approach that we could take that would actually get better results?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I would say two things there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When we have more emergency snow shovelers and we have the additional mechanized equipment, we will be able to get to more places more quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we're not necessarily saying, oh, we don't do that because that's DOT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If a place needs to be shoveled, we will shovel it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's just a question of how are we prioritizing the resources that we are allocating following a storm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As I've said, our priority following storms this upcoming winter is going to be bus stops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and those 20,000 priority corners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think we can talk about adding additional priorities, but once everything is a priority, then nothing is a priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we are going to focus on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are going to work with DOT to make sure that we have the right resources and equipment allocated to the assets that they also maintain.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'd be thrilled if they got their act together.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's just I've never seen it, and I've been in government a long time, and this is an issue that happens every single year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I hear it from council members.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I've heard it when I worked in the previous administrations.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I heard it from council members all across the city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The DOD does a terrible job here, and I've never seen it improve.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if you go to, like, the heart of South Williamsburg on Lee Avenue,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You cross the BQE overpass, and it's just a pile of ice and snow that is totally blocked off, and people can't walk from one commercial corridor to the next over the BQE because it's treacherous.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And DOT doesn't care or doesn't have the resources or isn't organized to do their job.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Whatever the issue is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I just think at some point we should take this out of their responsibility, and you all should just be responsible for it, and it should be Department of Sanitation's job to do it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we know it will get done that way because right now it's just complaining year after year and nothing changing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez asks about the current condition and average age of DSNY's snow equipment fleet, including plows, salt spreaders, and front-end loaders. DSNY officials provide average ages: collection trucks 5.1 years, dual bins 5.7 years, salt spreaders 7.5 years, with 12% of salt spreaders over 12-year service life.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez asks about DSNY snow equipment fleet age and condition

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is, speaking of these conditions, what is the current condition and average age of the department's snow equipment fleet, including plows, salt spreaders, and front-end loaders?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So our plows are just our standard collection trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And for our realtor collection trucks, our average age is 5.1 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our dual bins average age 5.7 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For our salt spreaders, those are a little bit older on average because they only work during the winter, so they have a longer life cycle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we also upgrade them every year, so we do a total rebuild of all of the key components.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those, the average age right now is 7.5 years.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What percentage of this equipment is beyond its recommended service life?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For collection trucks, it's a relatively small share.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For salt spreaders, it's only 12% are over the 12-year service life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But because the average age is seven and a half years, it does indicate that they're sort of in a group getting older and older.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, one of the things that we do every year is make sure that we are proactively ordering additional equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have many, many additional salt spreaders that we bring in every year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Last year, 48 salt spreaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: This year, another 20 on top of that have already come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we do what we can to try to stay on top of that.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez asks how many snow melters are operational versus planned. DSNY officials say they have 26 melters, some in winter upgrade cycle, and operated 13 last year, with capacity dependent on DEP sewer capacity.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez asks about operational snow melters

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How many snow melters are currently operational versus planned?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have 26.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Some of them are still in their winter upgrade cycle, so we couldn't necessarily put all 26 of them out today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we have some additional spares in that number, so we don't have 26 approved locations where we could operate melters if we wanted to because we have to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to work with DEP to make sure that the sewer has capacity to take the additional snow melt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But for example, last year we operated 13 melters, we had 26, so we were in a good spot.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez asks about the status of requirement contracts for additional snow equipment, salt, brine, and calcium chloride, and whether vendors are pre-qualified. DSNY officials explain they have requirements contracts with standby fees and separate emergency contracts, with a list of contractors ready.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez asks about DSNY snow equipment and supply contracts

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the status of the department's requirement contracts for additional snow equipment, salt, brine, and calcium chloride?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And has the department conducted outreach to additional vendors for snow emergency contracts?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Are these vendors part of a pre-qualified list?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we have two different types of contracts that we can bring equipment in off of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a requirements contract where there's a standby fee and they basically agree up front to deliver a certain amount of equipment with operators at any point during the season with 24 hours notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also have separate emergency contracts, which because they're emergency contracts, they don't exist yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we do a lot of preparation around making sure we have a list of contractors who can provide equipment and operators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We know where they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We know where we would assign them if we had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then we can really streamline that contracting process along with the controller's office when we get a declaration of emergency during the snowstorm.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez notes that South Bronx districts 1, 2, and 3 have fewer large spreaders and plowable trucks compared to other Bronx districts. DSNY officials explain these districts are geographically smaller and less hilly, so less equipment is needed, but service levels remain the same.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez questions disparities in Bronx snow plan equipment allocation

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: After reviewing the Bronx snow plan, it seems that there are fewer personnel and equipment in the South Bronx, particularly compared to other areas of the borough.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Specifically, districts 1, 2, and 3 have fewer large spreaders, plowable trucks, and plow bids overall compared to the South Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: to the other districts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you explain the reason for this difference?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So part of the reason is those are geographically some of the smallest districts in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So you look at some other districts like Bronx 12, for example, is geographically much larger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so the amount of equipment that it takes in order to have a plow assigned to every single plow route in the district is much greater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Bronx Community District 2, for example, is geographically quite small and the routes are

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm trying to think about how to explain it, but they're sort of compact, and so it's much easier for equipment to sort of operate through the routes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's a less hilly part of the Bronx than some of the other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So for all those reasons, there's less equipment assigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that the level of service is any less, and every sector in each of those districts will have a plow assigned as soon as the snow starts.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez asks if DSNY tracks missed street cleaning routes during alternate side parking windows. DSNY officials say they do track data and report it annually, and that many missed sweeps are due to parked cars blocking curb access, advocating for automated enforcement.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez asks about tracking missed street cleaning routes

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the department log or track data regarding missed street cleaning routes during alternate side parking windows?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Instances where a sweeper misses its window and cannot complete the route because the parked cars have returned.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the standard operational protocol or recourse?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So yes, absolutely we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And a lot of that data is reported in our annual sweep on YC report that we sent over to the council earlier this summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We also are routinely looking at 311 complaints for missed or inadequate sweeping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What we find is that in many cases, it's actually not missed sweeping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The street sweeper was there but could not get to the curb because of parked cars blocking it from doing its job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that's why, as we've said repeatedly in the past, we are big fans of the concept of automated enforcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because right now we don't have the number of officers that we would need to be able to do enforcement on every single block of ASP every single day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But with automated enforcement, we think compliance would improve pretty substantially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez introduces Council Member Shahana K. Hanif. She asks if delegating curb cut clearance to property owners meets ADA and Human Rights Law responsibilities. DSNY officials say property owners largely do their job, with enforcement for non-compliance.
chapters.title: Hanif questions DSNY on ADA compliance and property owner snow removal

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Council Member Huneeth?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs, and thank you for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm really grateful to hear some of my colleagues ask questions pertaining to New Yorkers with disabilities during snowstorms.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So New York City has the ultimate responsibility under the ADA and the New York City Human Rights Law to make sure pathways are fully accessible, including the removal of snow and ice from sidewalks and curb cuts.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is the current practice of delegating the clearance of curb cuts and pathways to property owners meeting those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think that, yes, in large part, property owners are doing their job and clearing their sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are cases where they are not, and we are doing enforcement to make sure that occurs.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And for those property owners who are not, do you have maybe like a worst offenders list or

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: keeping track in any sort of way as to which property owners might not be doing their share of the work?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, we certainly had properties that last year received repeated violations for failure to clear their sidewalk, whether that's failure to clear it at all or failure to maintain a clear sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's something that, you know, particularly last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we conducted enforcement in the same place multiple times in a row, there were some times where we just sent our staff out and cleared the sidewalk ourselves because we didn't want to wait any longer.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hanif asks about the largest violation amount for failure to shovel sidewalks. DSNY officials say fines range from $100 to $250, and they can charge for snow removal costs but rarely do due to documentation effort.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about fines for failure to clear sidewalks

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And what's the largest violation amount?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe it's 250.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That's it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: That's the highest a property owner is paying if they haven't shoveled their sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we can, under the administrative code, we can charge for the cost of snow removal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So if we use our employees to actually shovel the sidewalk, we can charge for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It does require us to document what those costs are and sort of come up with a billing procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's more effort than just shovel it and move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I don't think we've done that in many cases in the past, but it's something that we could look at in the future.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So the first violation is how much?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The first violation is $100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The range of penalties for failure to clear sidewalk is $100 to $250.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hanif asks what support the city offers disabled and elderly property owners to clear sidewalks. DSNY officials reiterate that sidewalk clearing is the property owner's responsibility, with NYC Service providing tools for community-based volunteer networks.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about city support for disabled and elderly property owners

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then what support for property owners does the city currently offer for those property owners who are disabled, elderly, to help them clear their sidewalks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the responsibility for clearing the sidewalk is theirs and theirs alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If you own property in New York City, you have to keep your sidewalk clean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You have to keep your sidewalk clear of snow and ice in the winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's a basic premise of owning property in a city like New York City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: New York City Service does provide tools for community-based organizations who want to try to connect volunteers to those who may need help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But at the end of the day, it is the responsibility of the property owners to clear their own sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Do property owners know that they have this resource available?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm speaking particularly about disabled homeowners and elderly homeowners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A lot of these networks are very, very localized, and so it's an existing...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Senior center that works with local volunteers who may already volunteer with that senior center and want to provide help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: during the winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, you know, it's a hyper-localized practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But again, the city is not offering a service to people who own property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If you own a property, you have certain responsibilities to maintain that property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Those responsibilities include clearing snow and ice in the winter.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So essentially the city doesn't...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Provide any additional services, this is all, you're talking about grassroots level kind of mobilizing that's happening, that could potentially be happening, because some neighborhoods don't have those resources.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hanif asks about meetings between the disabled community, City Hall, and the Council to ensure an inclusive snow plan. DSNY officials say they prioritize corners near transit and are in conversations with MOPD and DFTA, but no roundtable is currently scheduled.
chapters.title: Hanif asks about coordination with disability advocates for snow plans

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And currently, what

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: meetings or coordination is happening between the disabled community, City Hall, and the council to make sure that we've got a more inclusive and equitable plan for the next storms.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And is there a plan in place right now that is specifically about ensuring that disabled New Yorkers are able to get around during snowstorms?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So as I mentioned before, one of the things that we are doing differently this year is trying to prioritize which corners we are assigning our assets to, looking at bus routes, other transit stops.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Your assets to is, you're talking about like trucks and workers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Snow shovelers, sanitation workers, snow blowers, skid steers, plows, the whole range of things that we have available to help fight snowstorms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we're looking at a whole range of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I also mentioned before,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: that we are having conversations with DIFTA and the mayor's office for people with disabilities to make sure that we are prioritizing corners in areas that would be of particular importance to the communities that those agencies serve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At the end of the day, we can't prioritize everything, so prioritization has to mean something.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: You can't prioritize everything?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If everything is the same priority, then nothing is prioritized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So at the end of the day, we need to know which places to assign our assets first and then work through everything in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What we've said before is our priority for our resources this year is the 20,000 priority corners and all of the unsheltered bus stops across New York City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we can get through all of those locations, we will absolutely keep shoveling until there's nothing left to be shoveled or until Mother Nature gets there first and melts it for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's our approach.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is the department meeting with disabled New Yorkers or leaders?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I mean, there are either task forces or existing meetings happening maybe through MOPD, but it would be really, I think, beneficial for the department to be in a space

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: to hear directly from disabled leaders, advocates on the issue of...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Storms and addressing the priority concerns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's something that we've had a number of conversations with MOPD about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: would be happy to have more.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So currently there isn't a sort of maybe like something calendared that would be like a roundtable conversation between MOPD, the sanitation department, and disability advocates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's nothing immediately on the schedule, but we'd be happy to set something like that up.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.
